line.title: Follow the line. Inspect the connection.
story: A line joins two points. Follow its path.
Inspect: look carefully at where the line goes.
The arrow guides the eye from the label to its object.
line.rule: Name the relationship: a line runs along an edge, goes through an area, or connects one thing to another. The root spect is a useful clue in words about looking.

A2.model: The line connects A to B.
A2.note: Connect A to B: use to for the destination.

B1.model: The line connects the label to the picture, so the relationship is clear.
B1.note: So connects the visible choice to its result.

B2.model: The line that connects the label to the picture makes the reference explicit.
B2.note: The clause beginning with that identifies which line you mean.

check.question: Which sentence matches the line that joins the two points?
choices: The line connects A to B.
The line connects A at B.
The line connects A under B.
check.reason: Connect one thing to another: the line joins A and B.

transfer.context: Before printing, a designer inspects every connector to check that it points to the right object.
transfer.reason: Spect suggests looking; checking where each line points confirms that inspect means examine carefully.

line.prompt: Point to a line in a guide example. Say what it connects, divides, or guides.

color.title: One hue. A whole word family.
story: Many hues compete: red, blue, green, and gold.
Mono means one. The colors move into one hue family.
Different lightness levels; one hue. This palette is monochromatic.

parts.meaning: often makes an adjective: related to

family: monolingual / multilingual · one language / several languages
color.rule: Use word parts as clues, then check the picture and sentence. Monochromatic does not mean every swatch has identical lightness. Mono and chroma are Greek; multi is Latin.

A2.note: A hue is a color family, such as green.

B1.model: The palette is monochromatic because it uses lighter and darker greens.
B1.note: Because gives visible evidence for the design term.

B2.model: Although the values differ, the palette remains monochromatic because the swatches share a hue.
B2.note: Although signals a difference that does not change the conclusion.

check.question: The green swatches vary from light to dark. Why are they monochromatic?
choices: They must all have the same lightness.
They use every hue on the wheel.
check.reason: Mono points to one; the picture confirms one green hue with different values.

transfer.context: A multilingual notice gives the opening details in English, Bangla, and Arabic. What does multilingual mean here?
transfer.reason: Multi means many; the three named languages confirm the meaning. A useful reading habit, including for IELTS: word parts → context → likely meaning.

color.prompt: Choose a palette from the guide. Describe its hue relationship and say what helped you decode the term.

shape.title: Let the adjective show the shape.
story: Sharp corners: an angular shape.
The corners soften while the word ROUNDED rounds off.
Rounded is an adjective: a rounded shape.
shape.rule: An adjective usually comes before the noun it describes: a rounded shape, an angular shape. A/an follows the next sound: a rounded shape; an angular shape.

B1.model: The rounded shape has curved edges, whereas the angular shape has corners.

B2.model: The angular silhouette creates a different impression from the rounded one; audience context still matters.
B2.note: Describe the feature before interpreting the impression.

check.question: Which phrase correctly names a shape with sharp corners?
check.reason: Angular starts with a vowel sound; the adjective comes before shape.

transfer.context: The designer replaces an angular border with a rounded one. What changes?
choices: A flat image becomes a real object.
transfer.reason: Rounded describes the curved outline, not a change to the text or physical dimension.

shape.prompt: Compare a geometric and an organic example. Describe the outlines before guessing their effect.

texture.title: Say what a surface looks like.
story: Separate strands cross over and under.
The strands weave together through the letters.
Woven describes the visible result of weaving.
family: text · historically connected to weaving words together
texture.rule: A screen image can look rough, smooth, or woven. Use looks + adjective for visible evidence. Texture and textile share a Latin weaving history; this is a word family, not a rule for splitting every text- word.

A2.note: Looks + adjective: looks rough, looks smooth.

B1.model: The texture looks woven because the strands cross over and under.
B1.note: Woven is the irregular past participle of weave.

B2.model: The image suggests a woven surface; we cannot judge its actual tactile feel from the picture alone.
B2.note: Suggests distinguishes visual appearance from physical evidence.

check.question: You are describing a photo of rough stone. Which sentence keeps the claim visual?
choices: I can feel the stone through the screen.
check.reason: Looks takes the adjective rough. The photo shows appearance, not direct tactile experience.

transfer.context: A textile designer repeats interlaced strands in a fabric pattern. Which meaning fits textile?
transfer.reason: The weaving root is a clue; interlaced strands and fabric confirm the meaning.

texture.prompt: Choose two source textures. Describe how they look, then explain one use for each.

space.title: Make the invisible visible.
story: The word is invisible; only the surrounding area remains.
It becomes visible as the letters emerge.
Empty space makes the visible word easier to separate from its surroundings.
family: visible / invisible · can / cannot be seen
video · shares the Latin seeing family
space.rule: Vis/vid is a clue about seeing. In invisible, in- means not; in inspect, in- means into. Prefixes can have different jobs. Say less space / more space for an amount of empty area.

A2.model: There is more space around the word.
A2.note: Space is uncountable here: more space, less space.

B1.model: More space makes the word visible as a separate item.
B1.note: A separate gap can be counted: two spaces between groups.

B2.model: The negative space remains visible as the background and helps define the adjoining letterforms.
B2.note: Negative space is an empty area; it is not necessarily white or invisible.

check.question: You increase the empty area around a headline. Which sentence fits?
choices: There is more space around the headline.
There are more space around the headline.
There is many space around the headline.
check.reason: For an amount of empty area, space is uncountable: there is more space.

transfer.context: The pale caption is barely visible against the pale background. Which meaning fits barely visible?
transfer.reason: Vis suggests seeing; pale against pale and barely tell us it is difficult to see.

space.prompt: Point to occupied and empty areas in an example. Explain what the empty area helps you see.

form.title: Transform a shape. Explain the result.
story: A flat square has height and width.
Transform: the square changes into a shaded cube illustration.
Shading makes it look three-dimensional; the screen image is still flat.
form.rule: After makes + object, use the base verb: makes it look rounded. Form is a reusable root clue. Transform means change form; a rendered cube only suggests volume on a flat screen.

A2.note: Use look, not to look or looks, after makes it.

B1.model: Light and shadow make the flat shape look three-dimensional.
B1.note: A plural subject uses make: light and shadow make…

B2.model: The shading transforms our perception of the shape without adding physical depth to the screen.
B2.note: Separate suggested volume from actual physical volume.

check.question: Which sentence describes the shaded illustration naturally?
choices: The shading makes it look rounded.
The shading makes it to look rounded.
The shading makes it looks rounded.
check.reason: Makes + object + base verb: makes it look.

transfer.context: The icons are uniform: each uses the same outline and stroke weight. What does uniform mean here?
transfer.reason: Form gives a clue about shape; same outline and weight show that uniform here means consistent.

form.prompt: Use the experiment to add shading. Explain what makes the shape look solid.

typography.title: Read the word. Decode legible.
story: Blurred letters are difficult to read: illegible.
The letters sharpen and separate.
Legible: the word can be read clearly.
family: lecture · shares a historical reading family
legibility · how easily letterforms can be read
typography.rule: Legible concerns recognizing the letters. Readability also concerns reading longer passages comfortably. Compare specific versions: clearer than, easier to read than. Not every word beginning leg- belongs to this family.

A2.model: This word is easier to read.
A2.note: Easier to read compares two versions.

B1.model: The spaced letters are easier to read than the crowded letters.

B2.model: The individual letters are legible, although the dense paragraph still takes effort to read.
B2.note: Legibility and readability overlap, but the paragraph adds length and layout considerations.

check.question: Which sentence makes a clear comparison?
choices: This version is easier to read than the other one.
This version is more easier to read.
This version is easier to read that the other one.
check.reason: Easier is already comparative; use than to introduce the other version.

transfer.context: The notice is illegible because the letters overlap. What does illegible mean?
transfer.reason: Il- supplies a negative clue; overlapping letters confirm that the notice cannot be read clearly.

typography.prompt: Compare two type examples. Say which is easier to read in a small notice and point to evidence.

contrast.title: Show a difference. Join the ideas.
story: One word uses pale, light letters.
The other uses dark, heavy letters.
Whereas joins the contrast: this is light, whereas that is dark.
family: whereas / while · can contrast two ideas
contrast.rule: Use whereas or while to connect contrasting clauses. Describe a specific difference: lighter than, heavier than, different from. Contrast needs a relationship between things.

A2.model: This is light. That is dark.
A2.note: Two short sentences can express a contrast.

B1.model: This word is light, whereas the other is dark.
B1.note: Whereas joins complete clauses, not isolated adjectives.

B2.model: The light word recedes, whereas the heavier word attracts attention against this background.
B2.note: Qualify the effect with the actual viewing context.

check.question: Which sentence connects the two visible differences?
choices: This word is light, whereas the other is dark.
This word is light because whereas dark.
This word is light, whereas is dark other.
check.reason: Each side of whereas has a subject and verb.

transfer.context: The title is bold, while the supporting text is light. What does while do here?
choices: Says the event happens at the same time.
transfer.reason: While can express time or contrast; the two different type weights make contrast the relevant meaning.

contrast.prompt: Choose one contrast example. Describe both sides of the relationship, then explain its effect.

hierarchy.title: Primary first. Details next.
story: All three pieces of information compete equally.
Primary information becomes the first thing you notice.
Secondary and tertiary details follow in a useful order.
hierarchy.rule: Primary can mean main in importance, not only first in time. First, next, and finally organize your explanation of reading order. Check the context: primary colors use the same word differently.

A2.note: First introduces the first noticed detail.

B1.model: First, I notice the title. Next, I read the date. Finally, I find the place.
B1.note: Reading order should support what the viewer needs.

B2.model: The title has primary emphasis, while the date and location provide secondary and tertiary information.
B2.note: Importance depends on the brief, not a universal order for all posters.

check.question: The title is largest, the date medium, and the location smallest. Which explains the order?
choices: First the title, next the date, finally the location.
Finally the title, first the date, next the location.
Everything has the same visual importance.
check.reason: The sizes establish a visible order of emphasis.

transfer.context: The primary objective of the notice is to show where to register. What does primary mean here?
transfer.reason: Prim supplies a first/main clue; objective makes importance the relevant sense.

hierarchy.prompt: Describe the reading order in a source example. Say why that order fits the message.

alignment.title: Build a structure for pictures and sentences.
story: Scattered blocks have no shared starting edge.
Construct: the blocks build a shared structure.
Parallel visual edges and parallel verb forms make the sequence clear.
alignment.rule: The Latin struct family gives a building clue. English also needs parallel structure: compare verbs with verbs, or nouns with nouns. Read, compare, and explain share a grammatical pattern.

A2.note: Three base verbs give three clear instructions.

B1.model: Read the title, compare the versions, and explain the change.
B1.note: Keep all three actions in the same grammatical form.

B2.model: A shared alignment organizes the layout, while parallel verb forms organize the instruction.
B2.note: Parallel grammatical structure means matching forms, not necessarily matching line lengths.

check.question: Which instruction has parallel verb forms?
check.reason: Read, compare, and explain are all base-form verbs.

transfer.context: After the page file was lost, the designer reconstructed the layout from a sketch. What happened?
choices: Changed every word into a picture.
transfer.reason: Re- suggests again; struct suggests build. Lost file and sketch confirm rebuilding.

alignment.prompt: Find a shared edge in the guide. Explain it using two parallel actions.

balance.title: Both sides. Different ways to balance.
story: One side carries all the visual weight.
Both sides now contain the same-sized square.
Both squares are equal here. Other designs can balance unequal elements.
balance.rule: Both + plural noun takes a plural verb: both squares are large. One … the other distinguishes two items. Visual balance is perceived attention, not a measurement of physical mass.

A2.model: Both squares are the same size.
A2.note: Both refers to two, not three or more.

B1.model: One square is on the left; the other is on the right.
B1.note: The other identifies the remaining member of a pair.

B2.model: Although the elements are unequal in size, their position and contrast can still create visual balance.
B2.note: Although allows an unexpected result without claiming symmetry.

check.question: Which sentence describes the two equal squares correctly?
choices: Both squares are the same size.
Both square is the same size.
Both squares is the same size.
check.reason: Both takes the plural squares and the plural verb are.

transfer.context: Although the photograph is larger, the small dark title attracts strong attention. What does although signal?
choices: A result that may seem unexpected.
transfer.reason: Although recognizes that size alone does not determine perceived visual weight.

balance.prompt: Compare a symmetric and an asymmetric example. Describe both sides without treating visual weight as physical mass.

proximity.title: Near in the picture. Clear in the sentence.
story: A caption sits far from the picture it explains.
The caption moves nearer to its picture.
Proximity makes the relationship easier to identify.

parts.meaning: often names a quality or state

family: approximate · related historically; use context for its modern sense
proximity.rule: Proxim gives a nearness clue. Proximity is a noun. Clear English references work like clear image/caption groups: this caption, these pictures, the date beside the title. Avoid a vague it when two referents compete.

A2.note: This for one; these for more than one.

B1.model: The caption is close to the picture, so their relationship is clear.
B1.note: Name the caption and picture before using their.

B2.model: Moving the caption closer reduces the risk that readers associate it with the neighboring image.
B2.note: Reference can become ambiguous in both language and layout.

check.question: Which sentence clearly identifies the relationship?
choices: The caption beside the moon picture describes the moon.
check.reason: Naming the caption and picture removes competing references.

transfer.context: The registration desk is in close proximity to the entrance, so new visitors find it quickly. Where is the desk?
transfer.reason: Proxim suggests near; visitors finding it quickly at the entrance confirms the relationship.

proximity.prompt: Find a picture/caption pair. Explain which caption belongs to which image.

repetition.title: Use it. Reuse it. Make a system.
story: One reusable card sets a visual pattern.
Re- adds again: use the pattern again.
Different messages share the same visual system.
repetition.rule: Re- is productive in many English verbs: reuse, redesign, rearrange. The letters re at the start of a word are not always this prefix. Do not invent usefully meaningless splits such as re + peat for repeat.

A2.note: Reuse is a verb. Reusable is an adjective.

B1.model: Reuse the same heading style to connect the cards.
B1.note: To explains the purpose of reusing a feature.

B2.model: Repeating selected features creates consistency while allowing the messages themselves to vary.
B2.note: Consistency can include controlled variation; it need not mean copying every detail.

check.question: What should repeat to make a consistent set of three different notices?
choices: Every word of all three messages.
check.reason: A visual system repeats selected features while content can change.

transfer.context: The designer rearranges the same text blocks into two columns. What does rearranges mean?
choices: Arranges the blocks again in a new layout.
transfer.reason: Re- suggests again; the same blocks and new columns confirm a new arrangement.

repetition.prompt: Choose a repeated feature. Explain what stays consistent and what can vary.

simplicity.title: Shorten the sentence. Keep the message.
story: Extra words slow the sentence without adding needed meaning.
Brevity: the unnecessary wording becomes shorter.
He breathed deeply to calm himself. The action and purpose remain.

parts.meaning: a quality or state, in brevity

family: brief · short / a set of instructions, depending on context
simplicity.rule: Concision in prose preserves the action, purpose, and needed details while removing unnecessary wording. Brevity can help, but a necessary qualification should stay.

A2.note: Join us is a direct invitation.

B1.model: Join us Friday at 4 pm at the community hall.
B1.note: Keep the place if the reader needs it.

B2.model: The shorter invitation preserves the action, time, and place while removing redundant wording.

check.question: Which edit keeps the action and time from “We would like to invite you to join us on Friday at 4 pm”?
check.reason: The shorter sentence retains the invitation, day, and time.

transfer.context: Please abbreviate the month from September to Sept. to fit the label. What does abbreviate mean?
choices: Make the letters impossible to read.
transfer.reason: Brev suggests short; September → Sept. shows a shortened written form.

simplicity.prompt: Edit a wordy invitation. Point out what you removed and which essential details you kept.

function.title: Give the design a purpose.
story: An arrow has a shape and a color.
The arrow points to a named place.
Its function is to guide visitors to the entrance.
function.rule: Use to + base verb to state a purpose: to guide, to inform, to invite. Use so that + clause for an intended result: so that visitors can find the entrance. Word families help predict grammatical roles.

B1.model: The arrow is placed here to guide visitors to the entrance.
B1.note: To + base verb gives the purpose.

B2.model: The arrow and label work together so that first-time visitors can identify the entrance quickly.
B2.note: So that introduces the intended result, not a guaranteed outcome.

check.question: Which sentence states the arrow’s purpose clearly?
choices: It points right to guide visitors to the entrance.
It points right to guiding visitors.
It points right so that guide visitors.
check.reason: To + base verb: to guide visitors.

transfer.context: The notice gives information so that visitors can register before Friday. What is the intended result?
choices: Visitors learn a new texture name.
transfer.reason: So that introduces the intended result; it does not guarantee that everybody acts.

function.prompt: Name the audience, message, and intended action of a design. Explain how one element and one principle support it.
